body.html: The cardiovascular system circulates blood to every part of the body, carrying oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients and wastes; the heart contracts at least once a second and has its own electrical system. To unlock a term, break it into parts and read the meanings in order: suffix first, then prefix, then combining form(s): cardi/o + -logy = study of the heart. Specialists: cardiologist, paediatric and interventional cardiologist, cardiothoracic and vascular surgeon.

angi/o vessel (angiography: X-ray recording of vessels after contrast); aneurysm/o widening (aneurysmorrhaphy: suturing the dilated wall); aort/o aorta (aortostenosis: narrowing of the aorta); arteri/o artery (arteriosclerosis: abnormal hardening of arterial walls); arteriol/o arteriole (arteriolitis); ather/o fatty plaque (atheroma); atri/o atrium (atrioventricular); cardi/o heart (electrocardiogram: record of the heart's electrical activity); coron/o heart/crown (coronary); phleb/o, ven/o vein (phlebitis, venous); thromb/o blood clot (thrombolysis: breaking up a thrombus); vascul/o, vas/o vessel (vascular, vasospasm); ventricul/o ventricle (intraventricular: within a ventricle).

Endocardium (endo- within + cardi + -um): innermost lining of atria, ventricles and valves. Myocardium (my/o muscle): the muscular layer that contracts to pump blood. Pericardium (peri- around): a U-shaped sac secreting pericardial fluid; its visceral layer (on the heart) is the epicardium, its outer wall the parietal layer. Structures to label: right and left atria and ventricles, tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic valves, chordae tendineae, interventricular septum, apex, superior and inferior venae cavae, pulmonary trunk and veins, aortic arch; conduction: sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres.

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS): acute myocardial ischaemia from a clot in a coronary artery. Angina pectoris: chest pain from myocardial ischaemia (crushing, radiating to neck or left arm, sweating/diaphoresis), a warning of myocardial infarction (MI), death of myocardial cells. Coronary artery disease (CAD): coronary arteriosclerosis with atheromatous plaque. Cardiomyopathy: heart muscle disease. Murmur: abnormal sound from turbulent flow through a defective valve. Congestive heart failure (CHF): inability to pump enough blood. Cardiomegaly: enlargement of the heart. Endocarditis: infection of the endocardium. Rheumatic heart disease: after strep throat, mostly children. Arrhythmia (irregular rate or rhythm), bradycardia (slow), fibrillation (fast uncoordinated quivering; ventricular fibrillation needs defibrillation), asystole (no heartbeat: CPR). Vital signs: temperature, pulse, respirations (TPR) and blood pressure. Tests: CRP (inflammation), lipid profile, troponin (released when myocardial cells die), cardiac catheterisation, echocardiography and transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE).

Built terms: hyper/cholesterol/emia, tachy/card/ic, hyper/tension, cardio/centesis (puncture around the heart; strictly peri/cardio/centesis), trans/lumin/al, brady/cardia, hyper/lipid/emia, supra/ventricul/ar, a/rrhythm/ia, peri/card/itis, end/arter/ectomy, hypo/tens/ive, endo/card/itis, electro/cardio/graphy, thrombo/phleb/itis, cardio/myo/pathy, idio/path/ic, cardio/version. Drugs: ACE inhibitors (heart failure, hypertension), antiarrhythmics, antihypertensives, aspirin (prevents clots by keeping platelets from sticking), beta-blockers (angina, hypertension), thrombolytics (dissolve a blocking clot). Procedures: valve replacement, valvuloplasty (valvotomy), PTCA (percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty), CABG (coronary artery bypass graft); thoracotomy, sternotomy, cardiotomy, thrombectomy.

The endocrine system produces hormones, chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands directly into the bloodstream, which together maintain homeostasis (home/o constant + -stasis control): a constant internal environment. Hormone levels are measured in blood or urine. The specialist is an endocrinologist (endocrin = to secrete within); a certified diabetes educator (CDE) teaches patients to manage diabetes.

adren/o adrenal glands (electrolytes, metabolism, stress); gonad/o gonads: testic/o testicles (sperm), ovari/o ovaries (ova); pancreat/o pancreatic islets (blood sugar); parathyroid/o parathyroids (calcium); pineal/o pineal gland (sleep-wake cycle); pituit/o, pituitar/o pituitary (controls the other glands); thym/o thymus (immune reaction); thyr/o, thyroid/o thyroid (metabolism, growth, nervous activity).

The pituitary responds to neurohormones from the hypothalamus, a system of checks and balances. Anterior lobe: ACTH (adrenocorticotropic: adren/o + cortic/o cortex + trop change) stimulates the adrenal cortex; FSH stimulates oestrogen and ova growth, and sperm production; GH (somatotropic: somat/o body) regulates growth of bone, muscle and tissues; ICSH and LH stimulate ovulation in females and testosterone in males; prolactin (LTH, lactogenic) maintains milk secretion (lact/o milk, gen producing); MSH increases melanin and skin darkening (often in pregnancy); TSH stimulates the thyroid. Posterior lobe (stores hypothalamic hormones): ADH (antidiuretic) reduces water lost in urine and helps control blood pressure; oxytocin (oxy- swift + -tocin labour) stimulates uterine contractions and milk flow and controls postnatal bleeding (synthetic form: Pitocin).

Pineal: melatonin regulates the sleep-wake portion of the circadian cycle (24-hour biological rhythm). Pancreatic islets: control glucose (blood sugar, the body's basic energy) with glucagon (raises it) and insulin (lowers it). Thyroid: T3, T4 stimulate metabolism. Adrenals: cortisol and aldosterone. Gonads: testosterone; oestrogen and progesterone.

The digestive system is the gastrointestinal (GI) tract (alimentary canal) from mouth to anus: oesophagus, stomach, intestines, with accessory organs (liver, gallbladder, pancreas). Its job: break down food, prepare it for absorption and eliminate waste. Example: rect/o/plasty = surgical repair of the rectum; rect/o/vagin/al = pertaining to rectum and vagina; dia/rrhea = flow through (frequent watery stools).

dent/o, odont/o teeth (dentist; orthodontist: orth = straight); gingiv/o gums (gingivitis); gloss/o, lingu/o tongue (hypoglossal, sublingual); or/o, stomat/o mouth (oral, stomatopathy); ptyal/o, sial/o saliva (ptyalism, sialorrhea = hypersalivation).

pharyng/o throat (pharyngotonsillitis, pharyngitis, pharyngodynia/pharyngalgia); esophag/o oesophagus (esophagoscope = instrument, esophagotomy = incision, esophagotome = the cutting instrument); gastr/o stomach (gastroscopy = visual exam, gastrectomy, gastrotomy, gastritis, epigastric). The bolus moves by peristalsis; gastric juice and churning make chyme; gastro-oesophageal and pyloric sphincters. Peptic ulcer disease (PUD): ulcers named by site (oesophageal, gastric, duodenal). carcin/o cancer: carcinoma = malignant epithelial tumour; -ous = pertaining to.

Suffixes: -algia and -dynia pain; -emesis vomiting (hyperemesis, haematemesis = vomiting blood); -megaly enlargement (gastromegaly); -orexia appetite (anorexia); -pepsia digestion (dyspepsia = indigestion); -phagia swallowing/eating (dysphagia; aerophagia = swallowing air); -rrhea flow (diarrhea).

enter/o small intestine; duoden/o duodenum; col/o large intestine; rect/o rectum; an/o anus; hepat/o liver; chol/e bile, gall; cholecyst/o gallbladder; -lithiasis presence of stones (cholelithiasis); pancreat/o pancreas.

Immunology has earned many Nobel prizes and helps solve public-health problems: allergies and asthma, autoimmune diseases, HIV/AIDS, avian flu, viral hepatitis, COVID-19, cancer and immunotherapy. The lymphatic and immune systems work closely together to protect the body.

Three functions: (1) absorb fats and fat-soluble vitamins through the lacteals of the small intestine; (2) remove waste from tissues and help destroy pathogens; (3) return filtered lymph to the veins at the base of the neck. Often called the secondary circulatory system. Lymphatic capillaries: microscopic, blind-ended tubes one cell thick; lymphatic vessels: larger, deeper, with valves; they join into two ducts returning lymph to the veins. Lymph nodes: bean-shaped, with lymphocytes destroying bacteria, viruses and malignant cells.

Specialists: allergist (altered immune reactivity), immunologist (immun = protected), lymphologist (lymph), oncologist (onc = tumour).

Protects against pathogens (disease-producing microorganisms), allergens, toxins and malignant cells: first by preventing entry, then by destroying invaders. The antigen-antibody reaction (immune reaction) binds antigens to antibodies, labelling them for destruction. An antigen is anything the body regards as foreign (viruses, bacteria, toxins, transplanted tissue). Tolerance: acquired unresponsiveness to a specific antigen, or declining response to a drug with repeated use. B cells are lymphocytes that produce antibodies (immunoglobulins), each specific to one antigen. Autoimmune disorders: the immune system makes antibodies against its own tissues.

a-/an- not, without; aero- air; adeno- gland; angio- vessel; ante- before; anti- against; arthr- joint; cyto- cell; dys- malfunction; endo- inside; epi- on, above; erythro- red, RBC; exo-/extra- outside; intra- inside; hema- blood; hemi- half; hypo- insufficient; hyper- excessive; leuko- white, WBC; macro-/mega- big; micro- small; non-/un- without; oligo- few, small amount; para- next to; peri- around; pneumo- airways; poly- several; post- after; pseudo- false; pre- before; pyo- pus; sclero- hard.

Terminology is the study of specialised concepts and the terms that name them; medical terminology is the language used to describe the components and processes of the human body, medical procedures, diseases, disorders and pharmacology. It lets health professionals share vocabulary, understand lectures and reports, and speak as professionals. The key: word parts. Once you know how they fit together, most terms can be decoded.

A medical word is built from: a word root (the basic meaning, usually the body part: gastr = stomach), a combining form (root + combining vowel, usually o: gastr/o), a suffix (at the end; usually a procedure, condition, disorder or disease: gastr/itis, -itis = inflammation), and a prefix (at the beginning; usually location, time, number or status: peri/cardi/um). Example: peri/cardi/ectomy = surgical excision of all or part of the pericardium. Rules: a root cannot stand alone; a suffix must complete the term; a prefix always goes at the beginning.

Taking a term apart: start at the end (the suffix), work toward the beginning, give each part its meaning, then check with a medical dictionary. Not all terms are made of word parts.

Roots usually describe the body part: cardi (heart), nephr (kidney), gastr (stomach), thyr (thyroid), cephal (head), lingu (tongue), dent (tooth), dermat (skin), pancreat (pancreas), gyne (woman), chondr (cartilage), lip/o (fat), my/o (muscle), oste/o (bone), myel/o (spinal cord). Colours: cyan/o blue (cyanosis), erythr/o red (erythrocyte), leuk/o white (leukocyte), melan/o black (melanosis). Gastrodynia and gastralgia both mean stomach pain.

Three rules of word building: (1) a root links a suffix that begins with a vowel (gastr/itis); (2) a combining form (root + o) links a suffix that begins with a consonant (gastr/o/dynia); (3) a combining form links a root to another root to form a compound word, even if the next root begins with a vowel (gastr/o/enter/itis).

'Pertaining to' suffixes: -ac, -al, -an, -ar, -ary, -eal, -ical, -ial, -ic, -ine, -ior, -ory, -ous, -tic. Key suffixes: -algia pain; -ectomy surgical removal; -itis inflammation; -osis abnormal condition or disease; -ostomy surgical creation of an opening to the body surface; -otomy surgical incision; -plasty surgical repair (myoplasty); -gram a picture or record (angiogram); -scopy visual examination (arthroscopy); -rrhage/-rrhagia bleeding, abnormal excessive discharge (haemorrhage); -rrhaphy surgical suturing (myorrhaphy); -rrhea flow or discharge (diarrhea); -rrhexis rupture; -sclerosis abnormal hardening; -pathy disease; -cyte cell.

ab- away from (abnormal); ad- toward (addiction); dys- bad, difficult, painful (dysfunctional); eu- good, normal (eupnoea: normal breathing); hyper- excessive, increased (hypertension); hypo- deficient, decreased (hypotension); inter- between (interstitial); intra- within (intramuscular); sub- under (subcostal); super-, supra- above (supracostal); peri- around; pre- before (prenatal: before birth); endo- within; exo- out of.

Also useful: a symptom (e.g. pain) is felt by the patient; a sign (e.g. fever) is observed; a syndrome is a set of signs and symptoms. Abdominal regions: epigastric (above the stomach), umbilical (navel), hypochondriac (under the ribs), iliac (hip bone), hypogastric (below the stomach).

The skeletal system comprises bones, bone marrow, cartilage, joints, ligaments, synovial membrane and fluid, and bursae. Functions: framework, support and protection of organs, movement (with muscles, ligaments, tendons), calcium storage, and blood-cell formation in red marrow inside spongy bone. A long bone has proximal and distal epiphyses, a diaphysis of compact bone around the medullary cavity (yellow marrow), with periosteum outside and endosteum inside. Example: hydr/arthr/osis = swelling of a joint from excess fluid.

arthr/o joint (arthritis, arthrogram: X-ray after contrast injection into a joint, arthroscopy); burs/o bursa (bursitis); oste/o, oss/e, oss/i, ost/o bone (osteoporosis: bone removed faster than replaced; osteopenia); my/o muscle (myology); chondr/o, chondr/i cartilage (chondropathy); lip/o fat (lipoma: benign fatty lump); myel/o marrow or spinal cord (myeloma, myelopathy); hem/a blood (haemarthrosis: blood in a joint); neur/o nerve (neurolysis: freeing a nerve); ten/o, tendin/o tendon (tendonitis, tenolysis); ankyl/o crooked, stiff; cost/o rib; crani/o skull; kyph/o hump; lord/o swayback; scoli/o curved; spondyl/o vertebra; synovi/o synovial membrane or fluid. Regional: cleido- clavicle, gleno- glenoid cavity, om- scapula/shoulder (omarthrosis), humero- humerus, brachio- arm, carpo- wrist, palmar palm, digital and -dactyly finger (syndactyly, hexadactyly).

hyper/hypo (hypertrophy), supra/infra (supraspinatus, infraspinatus), macro/micro, poly/mono (polyarthritis, monoarthritis), dys, epi (epicondyle, epicondylitis), sub (subscapularis), brachy/dolicho short/long (brachydactyly), pre/post (preoperative), hydr- fluid, peri- around (periscapular), inter- between (interphalangeal), tetra- four (tetraplegia), trans- across (transtibial), allo- same species other individual (allograft), auto- same individual (autograft), xeno- other species (xenograft), ortho- straight (orthopaedics), sclero- hard, para- alongside (paraplegia), pan- all, necro- dead (necrosis), endo- inside (endoscopy).

-logy study (osteology); -plegia paralysis (paraplegia, tetraplegia); -esthesia sensation (paraesthesia); -gram recording; -sis process (arthrosis); -penia deficiency (osteopenia); -rrhagia excessive flow; -synthesis connection (osteosynthesis); -therapy treatment (sclerotherapy); -ectomy removal; -rrhaphy suture/repair (capsulorrhaphy); -lysis freeing, loosening (neurolysis, tenolysis); -desis binding, fusion (arthrodesis).

The nervous system has two parts: the central nervous system (CNS): brain and spinal cord, which receive and process information and regulate all bodily activity; and the peripheral nervous system (PNS): 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves, carrying signals to and from the CNS. Neurology treats diseases of the brain, cord and nerves; psychiatry treats mental, emotional and behavioural disorders.

Three connective-tissue membranes enclose the brain and cord (singular meninx). Dura mater ('hard mother'): thick, tough, outermost; lines the skull. In the spine the epidural space (between vertebral walls and dura) holds cushioning fat. The subdural space lies between dura and arachnoid. Arachnoid ('spider-like'): middle, web-like, loosely attached. The subarachnoid space (below arachnoid, above pia) contains cerebrospinal fluid. Pia mater ('tender mother'): delicate, vascular, innermost.

cerebr/o cerebrum (cerebrospinal; cerebrosclerosis); encephal/o brain (encephalitis); gli/o glue, neuroglia (glioma: tumour of glial tissue); mening/o meninges (meningocele: sac-like protrusion of meninges through skull or spine; -cele = hernia, swelling); myel/o spinal cord or bone marrow (myelalgia, myelitis, myelomalacia = softening, myeloma = tumour of bone marrow, myelopathy, myelotome); neur/o nerve (neurolysis = destruction; neuralgia = nerve pain; neuritis; neuroma = nerve tumour; neuropathy).

-paresis partial paralysis (hemiparesis: one side); -phasia speech (aphasia: absence of speech); -plegia paralysis (quadriplegia: all four limbs; hemiplegia: one side); -malacia softening; -lysis destruction, loosening; -cele hernia. Built words: aneurysmectomy (excision of an aneurysm), cerebrosclerosis (hardening of the cerebrum), polyneuritis, meningomalacia (softening of meninges), neuroma (benign nerve-tissue tumour). Eye and ear challenge words: iridalgia (pain in the iris), blepharitis (eyelid inflammation), dacryo/lacrimal terms, ophthalmology, blepharoedema, labyrinthotomy, iridopathy, retinectomy.

Genitalia are the reproductive organs and associated structures: external (outside the body cavity) and internal (protected within). The perineum is the surface region between the pubic symphysis and the coccyx. The male system produces sperm and delivers them so that one can unite with an ovum; some male structures also belong to the urinary system. A urologist treats the male genitourinary and female urinary systems (ur = urine); an obstetrician cares for pregnancy and birth.

Male: penis (pen/i, phall/i); testicles (orch/o, orchid/o, test/i, test/o): produce sperm and testosterone; scrotum, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory duct, prostate, bulbourethral glands, urethra, seminiferous tubules. Female: ovaries (oophor/o, ovari/o): ova and hormones; fallopian tubes (salping/o): catch the ovum, site of fertilisation; uterus (hyster/o, metr/o, metri/o, uter/o): protects the developing child; vagina (vagin/o, colp/o): intercourse, menstrual flow, birth canal; placenta (placent/o): nutrient and waste exchange. Uterine layers: perimetrium (outer), myometrium (muscular middle), endometrium (inner). The cervix (cervic/o) extends into the vagina via the cervical canal and os.

Other word parts: -gravida pregnant; gynec/o woman; mast/o breast; men/o menstruation; ov/o egg; -para to give birth; -pexy surgical fixation.

Endometriosis, epididymitis, episiotomy (incision of the perineum at birth), galactorrhea (milk flow), gonorrhea, haematospermia (blood in semen), hydrocele, hypomenorrhea and oligomenorrhea (scanty/infrequent periods), menometrorrhagia (excessive bleeding during and between periods), metrorrhea, leukorrhea (whitish discharge), hysterectomy, hysteroscopy, hysterosalpingography, mastalgia (breast pain), mastopexy (breast lift), menarche (first period), perimenopause, neonate (newborn), nulligravida (never pregnant), nullipara (never given birth), oophorectomy, orchidectomy, orchiopexy (fixing an undescended testis), ovariorrhexis (rupture of an ovary), fibroadenoma, fibrocystic breast disease.

The respiratory system delivers air to the lungs, transfers oxygen to the blood, expels carbon dioxide and a little water, and produces the airflow through the larynx that makes speech possible. Example of word analysis: poly/somno/graphy: recording physiological activity during sleep, to detect sleep apnoea. Specialists: otolaryngologist (ENT) (ot/o ear, laryng/o larynx), pulmonologist (pulmon = lung), thoracic surgeon.

nas/o and rhin/o nose; somn/o sleep; spir/o to breathe; pharyng/o throat (pharynx); laryng/o larynx; bronch/o bronchus; ox/o oxygen; phon/o sound or voice; pleur/o pleura; pneum/o, pneumon/o, pulmon/o lung (or air); trache/o trachea; capn carbon dioxide; -pnea breathing; -thorax chest; -ectasis stretching, dilation. Structures: nasal cavity, pharynx (nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx), epiglottis (lid over the laryngopharynx entrance), larynx and vocal cords, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles (smallest divisions of the bronchial tree), alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli; mediastinum (holds heart, aorta, oesophagus, trachea); visceral pleura (innermost) and parietal pleura; frontal sinuses just above the eyebrows; the diaphragm relaxes during exhalation.

Eupnea normal breathing; apnea temporary absence of breathing (common in premature infants); bradypnea slow (under 10/min); tachypnea rapid (over 20/min); Cheyne-Stokes respiration: alternating rapid/shallow and slow breathing or apnoea (coma, near death). Epistaxis: nosebleed. Voice: aphonia (loss of voice), dysphonia (difficulty speaking, hoarseness), laryngitis. Asphyxia: suffocation. Cyanosis: bluish skin from lack of oxygen. Hypercapnia: CO₂ build-up. Hypoxemia: low blood oxygen. Respiratory failure: dangerously low O₂ or high CO₂. Respiratory rate is a vital sign; sounds include rales, rhonchi and stridor (harsh high-pitched sound on inspiration from blockage).

Upper: URI (common cold, often rhinovirus), allergic rhinitis, croup (children: laryngeal obstruction, barking cough, stridor), diphtheria (toxin damages heart and nerves; vaccine), influenza, pertussis (whooping cough: paroxysmal cough then noisy inspiration; DPT vaccine), rhinorrhea (runny nose), sinusitis. Trachea and bronchi: tracheorrhagia (bleeding), bronchiectasis (permanent dilation), bronchorrhea. Pleura: pleurodynia, pleural effusion (excess fluid prevents full expansion), pyothorax/empyema (pus), haemothorax (blood), pneumothorax (air: lung collapse). Lungs: ARDS, atelectasis (incomplete expansion), pulmonary oedema (often heart failure), pulmonary embolism (sudden blockage, often by a clot from leg or pelvis), pneumorrhagia, tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis; haemoptysis), pneumonia: bronchopneumonia (localised, bronchioles) vs lobar pneumonia (whole lobes; 'double' if both lungs); asthma (episodes of breathlessness, cough, wheezing). Procedures: tracheotomy (incision) vs tracheostomy (stoma for a breathing tube).

The integumentary system (integument = to cover) is the skin and its related structures. The skin, about 2 square yards in an adult, is the largest organ: it covers the body, waterproofs it and prevents fluid loss, blocks pathogens (first line of immune defence), is the main receptor for touch, and helps make vitamin D from ultraviolet light while screening harmful UV. Specialists: dermatologist (skin) and plastic surgeon (restoration and reconstruction; -plasty = surgical repair), including aesthetic surgery.

Skin: cutane/o, dermat/o, derm/o; layers: epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous layer. Sebaceous glands (seb/o): secrete sebum to lubricate and discourage bacteria. Sweat glands (hidr/o): regulate temperature and water, excrete wastes. Hair (pil/i, pil/o): limits heat loss. Nails (onych/o, ungu/o): protect the last bone of each digit; parts: nail body, free edge, lunula, cuticle, nail bed.

More roots: hirsut/o hairy, rough; kerat/o horny, hard; lip/o fat; melan/o black; myc/o fungus; py/o pus; rhytid/o wrinkle; urtic/o rash, hives; xer/o dry; erythr/o red.

Acne vulgaris ('common acne'): chronic inflammatory disease with pustules from sebum overproduction around the hair shaft, triggered by puberty hormones but also in adults. Comedo (plural comedones): non-infected lesion of sebum and keratin in a follicle; closed = whitehead, open (oxidised plug) = blackhead. Sebaceous cyst: closed sac under the skin with yellow fatty material. Seborrhea: excessive sebum (seb/o + -rrhea). Lesions: crust (dried serum and debris), macule (flat discoloured lesion under 1 cm), papule (small solid raised lesion).
